newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Jamaica tells U.S. to prove drugs charges.
newsitem.headline: Jamaica tells U.S. to prove drugs charges.

text.p: Prime Minister P.J. Patterson on Wednesday challenged the U.S. government to prove its charge that Jamaican politicians were involved with drug barons or to retract the accusation.
He also said Jamaica would not yield on its position that a drug interdiction accord proposed by Washington would violate Jamaica's sovereignty.
Patterson was responding in parliament to statements made on Monday by Patricia Hall, the U.S. State Department's director of Latin American and Caribbean drug enforcement programmes.
Hall alleged that "at least one elected representative" in Jamaica maintained regular contact with drug traffickers and the government refused to take any action against the person.
She also said Jamaica had been warned it faced joining Colombia in having its drug interdiction efforts decertified, which would result in cuts in U.S. aid.

Patterson denied Jamaica was refusing to prosecute anyone either for political reasons or fear of reprisals, saying he regarded such accusations as "extremely damaging" and had sent a protest to the U.S. Embassy.
He said his government would request any information Washington had on the matter.
"If the allegation cannot be substantiated, then the only honourable course would be unequivocal retraction," he said.

Jamaica would not yield its position that an agreement to allow U.S. drug enforcement officials to operate in Jamaican territorial waters and airspace "must not infringe our sovereign rights", Patterson said. Hall said there had been no progress in talks on such an accord.
"We find it difficult to accept that negotiations should proceed with a threat of decertification hanging over our heads," Patterson said.
If Jamaica were decertified, U.S. aid, which in 1995 totalled just over US$40 million in grants and loans, would be cut in half.

The prime minister quoted from the U.S. State Department's March 1996 report, which said Jamaican cocaine seizures had tripled in 1995 and that cooperation in law enforcement was at its "highest levels in five years."
Patterson said under such circumstances, decertification would be "totally unwarranted."
